Eggs deposited by the Cuban tree frog typically hatch after an incubation period of approximately 1.5 days [ab = approximately 1.5 days] when maintained at a temperature of 29 °C [T = 29 °C], a brevity that underscores the rapid embryonic development characteristic of this invasive hylid. The resulting hatchlings emerge at a remarkably small size, with each neonate weighing just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams] upon hatching, a value derived from the spherical egg diameter of roughly 2 millimeters and reflecting the extreme altricial state of the newly emerged tadpole. This minimal initial mass necessitates a swift transition to exogenous feeding to fuel subsequent growth, and under optimal rearing conditions, the free-swimming larva progresses steadily through its Gosner stages. The combination of a very short incubation time and a tiny hatchling mass constitutes a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid population turnover, a trait that has likely facilitated the species' successful establishment across diverse wetland habitats throughout its introduced range in Florida and the Caribbean.

At a constant temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the aquatic larvae of the Cuban tree frog complete their development and undergo metamorphosis approximately 21 days after hatching . This duration from egg emergence to the terrestrial froglet stage is relatively compressed compared to many native North American hylids, allowing multiple cohorts to be produced within a single wet season. The metamorphic event itself involves the coordinated resorption of the tail and gills, the development of functional lungs, and the keratinisation of the skin, all of which prepare the individual for a terrestrial existence. Following this transition, the post-metamorphic individual enters a period of rapid somatic growth as a juvenile, during which it must accumulate sufficient body mass and energy reserves to survive the often drier conditions that follow the rainy months. The precise timing of metamorphosis can be influenced by local environmental factors such as pond drying rate, food availability, and density-dependent competition among conspecific tadpoles.

Under the same thermal regime of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], female Cuban tree frogs reach sexual maturity at approximately 255 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 255 days following metamorphosis]. This relatively short interval from the completion of larval development to reproductive activation enables females to contribute offspring within their first year of life, a fecund life-history trait common among invasive amphibian species. Upon reaching maturity, females display a substantial maximum body mass, with the ultimate wet weight for females attaining up to 57 grams [Wwi = up to 57 grams], a size that considerably exceeds that of most native tree frogs in the southeastern United States and confers a significant competitive advantage. The acquisition of this large adult body size is fueled by a highly generalist diet that includes not only insects and other invertebrates but also smaller amphibians, including members of its own species, reflecting a pronounced degree of intraguild predation that further bolsters its invasive potential.

The basal metabolic rate of resting adult Cuban tree frogs has been measured at 0.0027 milliliters per hour [JOi = 0.0027 milliliters per hour] when the animals are maintained at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This relatively low rate of oxygen consumption, quantified under standard laboratory conditions at this specific temperature, is consistent with the general metabolic scaling patterns observed across large-bodied hylids and reflects the relatively sedentary, ambush-foraging strategy that characterizes the species outside of breeding bouts. The resting metabolic expenditure occupies a small fraction of the daily energy budget, allowing most assimilated energy to be channeled into growth and reproductive output rather than being consumed by high maintenance costs. When compared to smaller sympatric anurans, the Cuban tree frog exhibits a somewhat lower mass-specific metabolic rate, a pattern that aligns with broader macroecological rules linking body size to metabolic intensity and that may contribute to its ability to tolerate a wider range of environmental temperatures without incurring prohibitive energetic demands.

In the context of reproduction, female Cuban tree frogs can achieve a remarkable maximum annual reproductive output, producing approximately 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and laying around 365 clutches per year [F_R_i = around 365 clutches per year], yielding a high daily fecundity when averaged across the entire breeding season and assuming continuous activity at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This high reproductive throughput is typically realized through the repeated deposition of large, gelatinous egg masses, with individual clutches containing several thousand eggs, and a single female may produce multiple clutches across the extended breeding season. The species' maximum lifespan has been recorded at 12.9 years [am = 12.9 years] under favorable conditions, a value that places it among the longer-lived anurans and is particularly noteworthy given its rapid maturation and high reproductive output at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This combination of a long adult lifespan and a high daily egg production rate generates an enormous lifetime fecundity, allowing even modest populations to expand rapidly and to recover quickly from localized disturbances, a demographic profile that has made the Cuban tree frog one of the most successful amphibian invaders in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.
